Why Does an Old Implant Suddenly Feel High?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Many patients experience concern when a dental implant that has felt comfortable for months or years suddenly begins to feel high or prominent when biting down. This unexpected change can be unsettling, particularly when the implant has previously felt natural and well-integrated with your bite. Patients often search online for answers when they notice their implant feels different, wondering whether this indicates a serious problem or requires immediate attention.

Understanding why an old implant might suddenly feel high involves examining several potential factors, from changes in the surrounding teeth and gums to mechanical issues with the implant components. This sensation doesn't always indicate implant failure, but it does warrant professional assessment to determine the underlying cause and appropriate management.

This article will explore the common reasons why a previously comfortable dental implant may begin to feel high, the clinical factors that contribute to bite changes, and when professional dental evaluation may be beneficial for addressing this concern.

Why Does an Old Implant Feel High?

An old implant may suddenly feel high due to changes in the surrounding teeth, gum recession, loosening of implant components, or natural settling of adjacent structures. Professional assessment can identify the specific cause and determine appropriate treatment.

Common Causes of Implant Height Changes

Several factors can contribute to the sensation that an established dental implant has become too high or prominent in your bite. Understanding these potential causes helps explain why this change might occur after a period of normal function.

Loosening of the implant crown or abutment represents one of the most common mechanical causes. Over time, the screw that secures the crown to the implant may gradually loosen, causing the restoration to shift slightly upward. This movement can create the perception that the implant has become high, even though the implant itself remains stable.

Changes in adjacent teeth can also affect how your implant feels during biting. Natural teeth may shift position over time due to normal wear, grinding habits, or gradual movement. When neighbouring teeth change their position, the relative height of the implant may feel different, creating the sensation that it has become prominent.

Bone remodelling around the implant site continues for months after placement, and changes in the supporting structures can occasionally affect how the implant crown sits in relation to your bite.

The Role of Bite Changes and Occlusion

Your bite pattern, known clinically as occlusion, naturally evolves over time as teeth experience normal wear and subtle positional changes. These gradual modifications can affect how forces are distributed when you chew, potentially making a previously comfortable implant feel different.

Natural teeth have a periodontal ligament that allows microscopic movement during function, helping to absorb biting forces. Dental implants, however, are rigidly connected to the bone and cannot move in the same way. As your natural teeth experience gradual changes, the immobile implant may begin to contact differently during biting and chewing.

Grinding or clenching habits, particularly during sleep, can accelerate wear patterns on natural teeth whilst having minimal effect on the implant crown. This differential wear can gradually alter your bite relationship, making the implant feel increasingly prominent over time.

Age-related changes in jaw muscle function and bite force can also influence how implants feel during normal function, contributing to the perception that an established implant has become high.

Understanding Implant Component Issues

Dental implants consist of multiple components that work together to create a stable restoration. The implant fixture sits within the bone, whilst an abutment connects to the implant and supports the final crown. Each connection point represents a potential area where loosening might occur.

Abutment screw loosening is a recognised complication that can develop months or years after implant placement. The repeated forces of chewing and biting can gradually affect these connections, particularly in patients who grind their teeth or have particularly heavy bite forces.

Crown cement failure represents another potential cause when implants are cemented rather than screw-retained. The cement that secures the crown to the abutment may deteriorate over time, allowing slight movement that creates the sensation of height change.

Examining the integrity of implant components requires professional assessment, as these issues are not always visible to patients and may require specific diagnostic techniques to identify accurately.

When Professional Assessment May Be Needed

Several signs suggest that professional dental evaluation may be beneficial when an implant begins to feel high. Persistent discomfort during biting, particularly when the sensation doesn't resolve after a few days, warrants examination to identify the underlying cause.

Changes in your bite that affect multiple teeth or create jaw discomfort may indicate that adjustment is needed to restore proper occlusion. Difficulty chewing comfortably or avoiding certain foods due to implant prominence suggests that professional intervention might help.

Any mobility or movement of the implant crown requires prompt assessment, as this may indicate loosening of components that can typically be addressed effectively when identified early. Pain, swelling, or changes in gum appearance around the implant site should also be evaluated professionally.

Professional assessment allows for proper diagnosis of the specific cause, whether mechanical, biological, or related to changes in surrounding structures. Early identification often enables straightforward solutions that restore comfort and function.

Treatment Approaches for High-Feeling Implants

The appropriate treatment for an implant that feels high depends entirely on the underlying cause identified during professional examination. Mechanical issues such as loose screws may be addressed through tightening or component replacement to restore proper function.

Bite adjustment, known as occlusal equilibration, may be recommended when the implant crown contacts too heavily during biting. This involves carefully removing small amounts of material from specific contact points to restore balanced bite forces across all teeth.

When surrounding teeth have shifted position, correcting bite alignment may occasionally be considered to improve overall occlusion, though this represents a more comprehensive approach typically reserved for significant changes.

Replacement of worn or damaged implant components may be necessary when mechanical failure has occurred. Modern implant systems are in many cases designed to allow component replacement with minimal disruption to the stable implant fixture within the bone.

The specific treatment approach should always be determined through clinical examination and assessment of individual circumstances, as each situation presents unique considerations.

Prevention and Ongoing Implant Care

Maintaining optimal implant health through consistent oral hygiene helps preserve the stability of surrounding tissues and reduces the risk of complications that might affect how your implant feels. Regular brushing, flossing, and professional cleaning support long-term implant success.

Protecting your implant through awareness of habits that create excessive forces, such as grinding or clenching, can help preserve component integrity. A nightguard may be recommended for patients who grind their teeth during sleep, reducing stress on implant components.

Regular dental check-ups allow for monitoring of implant stability and early identification of any changes that might affect function. Professional assessment can detect loosening or other issues before they become symptomatic, often enabling simpler treatment approaches.

Following professional recommendations for implant maintenance helps ensure optimal long-term function and comfort. This includes appropriate cleaning techniques and regular monitoring appointments.

Understanding normal implant function helps patients distinguish between minor variations in sensation and changes that may benefit from professional assessment.

Key Points to Remember

  • Sudden height sensation in old implants often results from component loosening or bite changes
  • Natural teeth continue to move and wear over time, affecting how immobile implants feel
  • Mechanical issues like loose abutment screws can typically be addressed straightforwardly
  • Professional assessment helps identify the specific cause and appropriate treatment approach
  • Regular maintenance and monitoring support long-term implant comfort and function
  • Early intervention often enables simpler solutions than waiting for problems to worsen

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a dental implant actually become higher over time?

The implant itself doesn't typically move upward once integrated, but loosening of components or changes in surrounding structures can create this sensation. Professional examination can determine whether actual height change has occurred or if other factors are responsible for the feeling of prominence during biting.

How serious is it when an old implant suddenly feels high?

This concern ranges from minor bite adjustments to component replacement, depending on the underlying cause. Many cases involve straightforward solutions such as tightening loose screws or minor bite adjustment. However, proper diagnosis through professional assessment ensures appropriate treatment and prevents potential complications.

Why might my implant feel fine some days but high on others?

Variable sensations can result from temporary gum swelling, changes in jaw muscle tension, or slight component movement that becomes more noticeable under certain conditions. Grinding habits during sleep might also create morning sensitivity that improves throughout the day as muscles relax.

Will a high-feeling implant damage my other teeth?

Improper bite forces from a high implant can potentially create excessive pressure on surrounding teeth over time. Professional assessment and appropriate adjustment help ensure balanced force distribution across all teeth, protecting both the implant and neighbouring natural teeth from unnecessary stress.

How long should I wait before seeking help for a high-feeling implant?

Persistent sensations lasting more than a few days warrant professional evaluation, particularly if the feeling affects comfortable chewing or creates jaw discomfort. Early assessment often enables simpler treatment approaches and prevents potential complications from developing.

Can bite changes affect multiple implants at once?

Yes, changes in overall bite pattern or jaw alignment can affect how multiple implants feel simultaneously. Comprehensive assessment of bite relationships helps identify whether individual implant issues exist or if broader occlusal changes require attention to restore comfortable function across all teeth.

Conclusion

When an established dental implant suddenly begins to feel high, understanding the potential causes helps patients make informed decisions about seeking professional assessment. From component loosening to natural changes in bite patterns, various factors can contribute to this sensation without necessarily indicating implant failure.

The immobile nature of dental implants means they respond differently to bite changes compared to natural teeth, making professional evaluation valuable for identifying the specific cause and determining appropriate treatment. Early assessment often enables straightforward solutions that restore comfort and protect long-term implant success.

Maintaining regular dental care and being aware of changes in implant sensation supports optimal oral health and helps ensure that any issues are addressed promptly. Professional guidance provides the most reliable approach for distinguishing between normal variations and changes that may benefit from intervention.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
